title: Custer County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Custer County wells have a 200 ft median depth and 7.5 gpm median yield. See what that means for drilling cost, water levels and buying land here.
h1: Water wells in Custer County, Colorado
intro_html: Custer County wells are classic high-country mountain wells: most are drilled into fractured granite and gneiss, and depths and yields can change quickly from one ridge or valley to the next. The county has 6,853 wells on record, with 5,000 reporting a total depth and 2,708 reporting a pump yield. Understanding those numbers before you buy or build near Westcliffe, Silver Cliff, or out in the hills will help you budget realistically and spot higher-risk lots.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Custer County
sections.html: Across Custer County, the median well depth is 200 feet, with the middle half running from 115 to 335 feet. That tells you a lot of wells finish in the 100–300 foot range, but another chunk goes deeper into hard rock. About 17% of wells are under 100 feet, 49% are 100–300 feet, 29% hit 300–600 feet, and 4% push past 600 feet. The deepest on record is 2,058 feet, which shows how stubborn fractured-bedrock can be in spots. For a driller’s bid, plan around that 200–335 foot band and accept that a few locations can surprise you on the deep side.

sections.heading: Well yield and how much water you can expect
sections.html: Production is generally decent here. The median reported yield is 7.5 gpm, with the middle half of wells between 5.0 and 11.0 gpm. Only 3% of wells report under 1 gpm, while 21% fall in the 1–5 gpm range. Most wells, 63%, produce between 5 and 15 gpm, and 12% are 15+ gpm. For a single home on an exempt well, anything around 2–5 gpm with decent storage is usually workable, so these numbers are encouraging. Still, that 3% under 1 gpm is the “problem well” slice you want to avoid by checking nearby permits before committing to a lot.

sections.heading: Water table depth and long-term trend
sections.html: Static water levels in Custer County are moderate for mountain country. The median depth to water is 80 feet, with the middle half running from 53 to 145 feet below ground. Looking at medians by decade, measurements sit at 80 feet in the 1980s, 75 feet in the 1990s, 91 feet in the 2000s, 67 feet in the 2010s, and 80 feet in the 2020s. That pattern bounces around but doesn’t show a steady long-term drop. In practice, expect the pump intake to be set well below those levels for drought margin, especially in fractured rock where water levels can move quickly with seasons and pumping.

sections.heading: Who’s been drilling here and when
sections.html: Custer County’s well history ramps up sharply after the 1960s. Records show 42 permits in the 1950s and 45 in the 1960s, then a jump to 539 in the 1970s and 842 in the 1980s. Activity peaks with 1,701 permits in the 1990s and 1,384 in the 2000s, then tapers to 742 in the 2010s and 636 so far in the 2020s. The newest permits run through 2026. Nequette Drilling (Nequette, David J.) has 1,561 wells in the records, Arkansas Valley Drilling (Moore, Todd A.) has 1,106, and Young'S Drilling & Pump Services (Young, Robert F.) has 582. That long permit history gives you good nearby examples to study before drilling.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Custer County
sections.html: Here you’re drilling into fractured mountain bedrock, typically priced around $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 200 foot median depth, that puts the bare drilled hole in the ballpark of $13,000–$20,000. By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished domestic well usually lands around $19,000–$32,000 at that depth. If your location ends up closer to the upper-middle range around 335 feet, costs climb right along with it. When you budget for land, assume at least the median-depth cost and keep some room for going deeper than expected.

sections.heading: Risks to check: low yield, contamination, and siting
sections.html: Custer County’s fractured-bedrock aquifer is unpredictable, so that 3% of wells under 1 gpm and 21% between 1–5 gpm matter. On a marginal-yield lot, you may need storage or to live within tighter water limits. There are also mapped environmental issues to be aware of: about 8 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, roughly 2,110 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. None of that means your specific well is bad, but it’s a reason to review maps and test water. Plan well and septic layouts together so you maintain proper separation and avoid boxed-in building envelopes.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a well lot in Custer County
sections.html: Before buying land around Westcliffe, Silver Cliff, or the outlying valleys, pull the nearby well permits and note depths, yields, and static levels. Most wells here are for domestic or household use (about 89%), with some stock wells (21%), so you’ll usually be dealing with a standard exempt household well permit and its pumping limits. With 49% of wells between 100 and 300 feet and a median yield of 7.5 gpm, many properties are solid, but you still want site-specific information. Budget at least a median-depth well plus power and access, and write your contract so poor drilling results don’t leave you stuck.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Custer County, Colorado?
faq.a: Based on 5,000 wells reporting depth, the median well in Custer County is about 200 feet deep. The middle half fall between 115 and 335 feet. Around 17% are under 100 feet, 49% are 100–300 feet, 29% are 300–600 feet, and 4% go deeper than 600 feet, with the deepest recorded well reaching 2,058 feet.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Custer County?
faq.a: From 2,708 wells with reported pump tests, the median yield is 7.5 gpm, and the middle half of wells produce 5.0–11.0 gpm. About 3% of wells report under 1 gpm, 21% are 1–5 gpm, 63% fall between 5 and 15 gpm, and 12% are above 15 gpm. For a single home, that range is generally workable with proper system design.

faq.q: How deep is the water table in Custer County?
faq.a: Static water level measurements from 753 wells show a median depth to water of 80 feet, with the middle half between 53 and 145 feet. By decade, medians are 80 feet in the 1980s, 75 in the 1990s, 91 in the 2000s, 67 in the 2010s, and 80 in the 2020s, which suggests some variation over time but no simple, steady decline.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Custer County?
faq.a: In Custer County’s fractured bedrock, drilling typically runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the 200 foot median depth, that works out to roughly $13,000–$20,000 for the hole alone. A complete domestic well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical commonly totals around $19,000–$32,000 at that depth, with deeper wells scaling up from there.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Custer County?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. The area has about 8 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, roughly 2,110 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Many homes use wells safely, but you should test a new or existing well for bacteria, metals, and any contaminants of concern before relying on it for drinking water.
